t071.description: Categorise three months of bank transactions for a fictional small business in QuickBooks Online's free test company (or a free alternative such as Wave). The 180 transactions are supplied as illustrative data, and the chart of accounts and rules are given in the brief.
objectives: Handle transfers and owner draws correctly
t071.instructions:
Read the chart of accounts and the policy notes in the case data, and write a one-page cheat sheet of which vendors map to which accounts.
Set up a free test company (QuickBooks sandbox, Wave or a spreadsheet) with the chart of accounts and import the transaction CSV.
Categorise recurring items first (software subscriptions, rent, utilities) and create bank rules to apply them automatically.
Categorise the remaining transactions one by one, and split mixed items where the description shows more than one purpose.
Mark owner draws, loan payments and transfers correctly so they do not appear as expenses, and check that transfers between accounts balance.
Create the query list for items you cannot classify (vague descriptions, large unusual amounts) with the question you would ask the owner.
Run the profit and loss for the three months and review it for odd categories (for example meals larger than rent).
Reconcile the total of categorised transactions to the bank statement total and record the check.

brief.background: Bookkeeping accuracy depends on consistent categories. Mistakes in categorisation distort profit and tax reports, and the best practice is to apply rules consistently, mark uncertain items for the owner and never guess silently.
brief.problem: Categorise 180 transactions to the supplied chart of accounts, create bank rules for recurring items, and produce a query list for transactions that cannot be classified.
scopeIn: A query list for unclear items
A summary of expenses by category
brief.caseData:
Business (fictional): Riverbend Bike Repair. Chart of accounts: Sales, Parts purchases (COGS), Rent, Utilities, Software, Insurance, Meals, Vehicle, Bank fees, Owner draw, Loan payment, Uncategorised.
Transactions (sample of 180): 09/02 VELO PARTS LTD -412.60 | 09/03 SQUARE DEPOSIT +1,240.00 | 09/04 CITY POWER -86.15 | 09/05 TRANSFER TO SAVINGS -500.00 | 09/06 COFFEE HUT -14.20 | 09/09 JS SMITH -300.00 (no note) | 09/10 MONTHLY ACCT FEE -12.00.
Notes: Square deposits are sales net of fees; transfers to savings are not expenses.
acceptance: All 180 transactions have a category from the chart of accounts
Transfers and owner draws are not counted as expenses
Rules exist for recurring vendors
The query list explains every unclear item
Categorised totals reconcile to the statement totals

After about 4.5 hours: all categorised
After about 6 hours: reconciliation and report submitted

t072.description: Reconcile a six-month backlog of bank and credit-card statements for a fictional business using supplied illustrative statements and ledger exports. You match every item, identify timing differences and errors, and prepare six monthly reconciliation reports.
t072.instructions:
Open the statements and ledger exports in the case data and set up one workbook with a tab per account and month.
For each month start from the statement ending balance, add deposits in transit, subtract outstanding payments and compare the adjusted bank balance with the ledger balance.
Tick each statement line against the ledger line using date, amount and reference, marking matched items.
List unmatched items on each side and classify them: timing difference, bank fee or interest not yet recorded, error in the ledger or unknown.
Prepare adjusting journal entries (debits and credits) for fees, interest and errors, with explanation.
Check opening balances equal the prior month's closing and that no item is cleared twice.
Calculate the unexplained difference for each month (it must be zero after adjustments) and investigate any residual.
Summarise the recurring problems and recommend controls (for example weekly reconciliation or bank feed).
deliverables: Reconciliation workbook (XLSX), one tab per month and account

brief.background: A reconciliation proves that the books agree with the bank. Differences usually come from timing (outstanding cheques, deposits in transit), bank fees not yet recorded or keying errors. Unreconciled differences are a classic warning sign.
brief.problem: Produce six month-end reconciliations for two accounts that end with a zero unexplained difference, with a list of adjusting entries.
scopeIn: Reconciliation of one bank and one credit-card account for six months
scopeOut: Posting in a live accounting system
brief.caseData:
Account (fictional): Riverbend Bike Repair checking account. September statement ending balance $14,820.55. Ledger balance at 30 Sep $15,640.10.
Deposits in transit: $1,050.00 deposited 29 Sep, cleared 2 Oct. Outstanding cheques: #1048 $610.00, #1051 $239.55. Bank fee $18.00 not in ledger. Interest $4.10 not in ledger. Suspected error: ledger shows $1,480.00 but the statement shows $1,408.00 for a customer deposit (transposition).
(Five more months follow the same format in the supplied files.)
acceptance: Each month's adjusted bank balance equals the adjusted ledger balance
Outstanding items are carried forward correctly
Adjusting entries balance (debits equal credits)
The transposition error is identified and corrected
Recommendations refer to observed problems
milestones: After about 1.5 hours: workbook and first two months
After about 3 hours: all six months
After about 4 hours: entries and summary submitted

t073.description: Prepare a monthly management accounts pack for a fictional 12-person consultancy using supplied trial balance data: profit and loss, balance sheet, cash summary, and a written commentary with variance explanations against budget and the previous month.
t073.instructions:
Study the trial balance, budget and prior-month data in the case data and check that the trial balance sums to zero.
Map the accounts to the P&L and balance sheet lines and build the statements in Excel with formulas linked to a trial balance tab.
Check that assets equal liabilities plus equity and that the P&L profit equals the movement in retained earnings.
Prepare accruals and prepayments given in the notes (for example one month of rent prepaid) and show them as adjustments.
Calculate variances against budget and the prior month in amount and percent, highlighting those over 10 percent and $2,000.
Compute the KPIs (gross margin, utilisation, debtor days, cash runway) and a short cash bridge from opening to closing cash.
Write the commentary: headline result, the three largest variances with reasons based on the notes, cash position and actions for the next month.
Review the pack for consistency of numbers across pages and format it professionally.

brief.background: Owners rely on management accounts to decide on hiring, pricing and cash. A pack is only useful if the numbers are right, comparisons are meaningful and the commentary explains why things changed, not just what changed.
brief.problem: Produce a one-month pack with P&L versus budget and prior month, balance sheet, cash flow summary, KPIs and a two-page commentary.
scopeIn: P&L, balance sheet and cash summary from a trial balance
Budget and prior month variance analysis
KPIs: gross margin, utilisation, debtor days, runway
scopeOut: Bookkeeping adjustments beyond the ones listed

Firm (fictional): Northbridge Advisory, 12 staff. October: revenue $182,400 (budget $175,000; September $168,900); salaries $96,500; contractors $14,200; rent $9,800 (includes $9,800 prepaid for November: adjust); software $4,300; travel $7,100 (budget $3,000: client trip); depreciation $1,200.
Balance sheet at 31 Oct (illustrative): cash $212,000; debtors $146,000; fixed assets $38,000; creditors $41,000; VAT and payroll liabilities $52,000; loan $60,000; equity balancing.
Notes: one-off client trip; a $15,000 invoice outstanding 75 days.

Variances are correct and explained with causes from the notes
KPIs are defined and correct
Prepaid adjustment is reflected
Commentary is under two pages and ends with actions

t074.description: Design and configure an accounts-payable automation workflow for a fictional company using a free tool trial (Dext, Zoho Expense, or a Google Workspace plus Zapier set-up). You build invoice capture, three-way matching rules, approval routing and an SOP, and test it on 15 sample invoices.
t074.instructions:
Read the AP policy in the case data (approval thresholds, segregation of duties, payment terms) and draw the process flow.
Choose a free tool or trial and create a capture route (a dedicated email address or upload folder).
Prepare 15 sample invoices (generate PDFs from a template) including a duplicate, an invoice with a wrong total and one over the approval limit.
Configure extraction fields (supplier, number, date, total, tax) and confirm that the data are read correctly or corrected.
Create the approval routing: under $1,000 department head, $1,000 to $10,000 finance manager, over $10,000 two approvers, and ensure that the requester cannot approve their own.
Add duplicate detection (supplier plus number plus amount) and exceptions queue handling.
Run the 15 invoices through, record each outcome and time in the test log, and correct the configuration where results differ from the expected.
Write the SOP with the process diagram, roles, controls and what to do when an invoice is disputed.

brief.background: Manual accounts payable causes late payments, duplicates and fraud risk. Automation of capture and approval reduces cost per invoice, but only when approval limits, segregation of duties and exception handling are designed carefully.
brief.problem: Build a working workflow that captures invoices, extracts data, routes them by amount and department for approval, flags duplicates and posts to a ledger sheet, tested on 15 invoices, with an SOP.

Approval rules by amount and department

Test invoices: 15 PDFs: 10 normal, 1 duplicate, 1 total mismatch (lines sum to $1,180 but total says $1,810), 1 over $10,000, 1 missing PO number, 1 from an unknown supplier.

t075.description: Build a linked three-statement financial model (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow) in Excel for a real public company using its latest annual report from SEC EDGAR, with a five-year forecast and three scenarios. You document assumptions, include integrity checks and write a one-page summary.
t075.instructions:
Choose a company with simple operations and download its latest Form 10-K from SEC EDGAR; record the company, filing date and URL.
Enter three years of the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement as reported in a historicals tab, and check that totals match the filing.
Compute historical ratios (growth, margins, days receivable, inventory and payable, capex percent of sales) to guide the assumptions.
Build the assumptions sheet with drivers and a scenario selector (base, upside, downside) using CHOOSE or INDEX.
Forecast the income statement from revenue growth, margins and tax; build schedules for working capital, property and equipment, and debt with interest on average balances (avoid circularity by using opening balances or switch).
Link the balance sheet and derive the cash flow statement from the changes; set cash as the balancing line from the cash flow.
Create the checks sheet: balance sheet balances, cash ties, net income ties, no negative cash, with a master check cell on every tab.
Document each assumption and its rationale, and write a one-page summary of the three scenarios and the main sensitivities.

brief.background: A three-statement model is the base of most valuation and planning work. It is only trustworthy if the balance sheet balances in every period, cash flows tie to the balance sheet and each assumption is traceable.
brief.problem: Model a chosen mid-size public company (for example a US retailer or manufacturer with simple operations) from historical statements with a five-year forecast, base, upside and downside scenarios and a model-checks sheet.
scopeIn: Three years of historical statements from a 10-K
Debt, interest and working capital schedules
acceptance: Historicals match the 10-K exactly
The balance sheet balances in every forecast year in all scenarios
Cash flow ties to the balance sheet cash
All inputs are on the assumptions sheet with a rationale
The summary compares the three scenarios and key sensitivities
milestones: After about 6 hours: historicals and ratios
After about 14 hours: forecast and schedules
After about 20 hours: scenarios and checks
After about 24 hours: documents submitted

t076.description: Review sales-tax nexus exposure for a fictional online seller across US states, using the post-Wayfair economic-nexus thresholds published by the states and the Streamlined Sales Tax Governing Board. You analyse the illustrative sales by state, determine where registration is required and prepare a memo and registration plan.
t076.instructions:
Read the case data and list the seller's facts: product type, marketplace versus direct sales, physical presence and the sales by state.
Research each state's current economic nexus threshold and measurement period from its department of revenue website; record the URL and the date of access for each state.
Compare the annual sales and transactions per state with the threshold and mark states as nexus, approaching (over 80 percent) or none.
Handle marketplace sales: identify states where marketplace facilitators collect the tax so that the seller's own exposure is reduced.
Estimate the exposure for each nexus state: taxable sales since the date the threshold was first crossed multiplied by the combined average rate, stating the rate source and the assumptions.
Prioritise registration by exposure, by deadlines (some states require registration within a set number of days) and by the cost of compliance.
Check product taxability (clothing or digital goods differ by state) for the three highest exposure states.
Write the memo with the findings, exposure table, plan, assumptions and a clear statement of what you could not verify.
deliverables: Nexus analysis workbook with source URLs (XLSX)

brief.background: Since South Dakota v. Wayfair (2018) states can require remote sellers to collect sales tax after crossing economic thresholds, commonly $100,000 in sales or 200 transactions. Thresholds, measurement periods and marketplace rules differ, so a state-by-state analysis is needed.
brief.problem: Use the supplied annual sales data by state to decide in which of 15 states the seller has economic nexus, estimate the exposure and prepare a registration plan and a memo.
scopeIn: Exposure estimate with a stated method

inputs.title: Streamlined Sales Tax: remote seller state guidance

brief.caseData:
Seller (fictional): Hilltop Outdoor, sells camping gear through its own website. Annual sales (illustrative, state: sales $ / transactions): CA 212,000/1,450; TX 148,000/890; NY 96,000/610; WA 133,000/720; FL 74,000/430; IL 118,000/690; PA 101,500/540; OH 54,000/320; CO 86,000/470; GA 88,000/510; (5 more states follow the same format).
Marketplace: 20% of sales go through a marketplace that collects tax. No physical presence outside Oregon.
acceptance: Each state's threshold has a source URL and access date
Nexus determination follows the threshold and measurement period of that state
The exposure method is explicit and reproducible
Marketplace sales are treated properly
The memo states its limits and that it is not tax advice
milestones: After about 5 hours: research on thresholds
After about 10 hours: analysis and exposure
After about 15 hours: memo submitted

t077.description: Perform a due-diligence financial review of a real public company's recent acquisition target scenario using only public filings: analyse quality of earnings and working capital for a company you choose from SEC EDGAR (small reporting companies work best), and produce a report and an adjustments schedule as if advising an acquirer. No private data is used.
t077.instructions:
Select a smaller reporting company with a simple business from SEC EDGAR, download its 10-K filings for three years and the latest four 10-Qs, and record the sources.
Extract revenue, cost of sales, operating expenses, EBITDA and cash flow data into a workbook and reconcile to the reported totals.
Search the notes and MD&A for non-recurring items (restructuring, impairments, litigation, gains on sale) and list candidate adjustments with the page references.
Analyse revenue quality: concentration (customers over 10 percent), changes in recognition policy, deferred revenue and bad debt trends.
Build the adjusted EBITDA bridge from reported to adjusted with each adjustment explained and rated for reliability.
Calculate net working capital from the quarterly balance sheets, adjust for cash and debt-like items and show the trend, average and a proposed peg for a hypothetical deal.
Identify debt-like items (leases, deferred compensation, unfunded pensions, tax liabilities) from the notes.
Write the report with an executive summary, findings by area, a red-flags table rated high, medium or low, and the adjustments schedule.
deliverables: Workbook with the EBITDA bridge, adjustments and working capital (XLSX)

brief.background: Acquirers look past reported profit to the earnings that will continue: one-off gains, aggressive revenue recognition and under-investment can all flatter the numbers. Working-capital analysis shows how much cash is tied up and whether the seasonality is understood.
brief.problem: Analyse three years of public financial statements to produce an adjusted EBITDA bridge, a monthly or quarterly net working capital analysis from the quarterly filings and a red-flags list.
scopeIn: Quality of earnings analysis from filings
Adjusted EBITDA bridge and adjustments schedule
Net working capital trend and peg proposal
acceptance: Every adjustment has a page reference in the filing
The EBITDA bridge reconciles from reported to adjusted
Net working capital is calculated consistently each quarter
At least five red flags are rated and justified
The report states that only public information was used and the limits of that

t085.description: Draw bounding boxes on 1,500 street-scene images from the open COCO or Open Images datasets (re-annotating without looking at the existing labels), following a labelling guideline, so that your work can be scored against the reference annotations. You record quality and edge cases.
t085.instructions:
Install CVAT (cvat.ai free tier) or Label Studio (open source) and read the guideline in the case data.
Download a set of 1,500 street-scene images from Open Images V7 or COCO (pick images with the five classes), recording the licence of the dataset and image IDs.
Create the project with the five labels and set the box rules: tight to the visible extent, include occluded parts only when visible, minimum box size 16 pixels, no boxes for objects under 50 percent visible if fewer than 4 pixels...
Annotate in batches of 250 images, using shortcuts and tracking your speed in images per hour.
Every 250 images stop and review 10 random images to check for drift in your own box style.
Export the annotations in COCO format and compare a 150-image sample with the dataset's reference annotations by computing IoU and matching boxes at 0.5, then report precision, recall and mean IoU.
Log edge cases (heavy occlusion, reflections, partial vehicles) with the image ID and the rule you applied, and propose clarifications to the guideline.
Write a short quality report with the metrics and the guideline suggestions.

brief.background: Object detectors learn from annotations, and inconsistent boxes (too loose, missing small objects, labels that change between annotators) limit a model's accuracy. Annotation guidelines and quality checks are what make a dataset usable.
brief.problem: Annotate 1,500 images with boxes for five classes using the guideline, measure agreement with the reference labels (IoU) and report edge cases.
scopeIn: 1,500 images with boxes for car, bus, truck, person, bicycle
Annotation in CVAT or Label Studio
IoU comparison with the dataset's labels on a 150-image QA sample

inputs.note: Large public image dataset with licence information.

acceptance: 1,500 images are annotated with the five classes
Mean IoU against the reference on the 150-image sample is reported (target 0.75 or higher)
Annotation drift checks are recorded
Edge cases cite the rule applied
The dataset licence and image IDs are recorded

t086.description: Rate and rank AI chatbot responses for helpfulness, accuracy and safety using a rubric. You evaluate 60 prompt and response sets supplied in this brief's case data pattern (and ones you generate by prompting two public chatbots), write a short justification for each and log difficult edge cases.
t086.instructions:
Read the rubric in the case data and rewrite each dimension in your own words with one example of a score 1 and a score 5.
Create 60 prompts covering factual questions, advice, writing tasks, reasoning and some borderline safety requests (avoid anything harmful) and collect two responses to each from two public assistants or two settings.
For each pair score helpfulness, accuracy (verify facts using reliable sources), clarity and safety on 1 to 5, and choose the better response.
Write a 30 to 80 word rationale that cites specific features of each response rather than general impressions.
Verify at least 20 factual claims against authoritative sources and record the sources.
After a day, re-rate 10 pairs without looking at your first scores and compute the agreement.
Flag ten edge cases (both responses wrong, borderline safety, ambiguous prompt) with the issue and the way you resolved it.
Write a one-page summary of patterns in the responses (such as verbosity or confident errors) and suggestions to refine the rubric.
deliverables: Ratings workbook with scores, preference and rationale (XLSX)

brief.background: Human preference data are used to evaluate and improve language models. Useful ratings are consistent, justified and based on an explicit rubric rather than on style or length. Raters also need to recognise unsafe or deceptive content.
brief.problem: Score 60 response pairs on four rubric dimensions and rank them with a written rationale, reaching consistency on a repeat sample.
scopeIn: A consistency check on 10 repeated items
scopeOut: Writing the prompts for production use

Overall preference: A, B or tie. A confident wrong answer is worse than an honest 'I am not sure'.
acceptance: 60 pairs are scored with rationales that cite specifics
At least 20 facts are checked with sources
Repeat-rating agreement is reported and is at least 80 percent on preference
Edge cases are logged with how they were resolved
No harmful content is reproduced in the log

t087.description: Write a regression test suite for an LLM feature (a support-email summariser) that you implement with a public model API or an open model, including 40 prompts with expected behaviours, automated checks and an evaluation script that you run on two model settings.
objectives: Test properties instead of exact text
t087.instructions:
Create a Python project with a function summarise(email) that calls an open model (Ollama with a small model) or a public API using your own key, with two prompt versions in files.
Write 40 invented support emails covering normal cases, long threads, missing information, multiple languages, prompt-injection attempts and sensitive data.
For each email define expected properties: summary under 60 words, includes order number if present, no invented facts, refuses instructions inside the email, keeps the language of the sender.
Implement checkers: deterministic ones with regex and word count, a JSON-schema check for structured output and an LLM-as-judge for faithfulness with a rubric that you validate on 10 hand-labelled cases.
Write the runner that evaluates both prompt versions, repeats each three times at temperature 0.7 and reports pass rate per property and flakiness.
Review the failures, classify them (model error, bad test, ambiguous expectation) and fix tests that are wrong.
Add the suite to pytest with a threshold gate (fail if the pass rate falls under 90 percent).
Write a report comparing the prompt versions with pass rates, examples of regressions and recommendations.

brief.background: LLM outputs vary, so teams need tests that check properties (is the summary short, does it include the order number, does it refuse to invent facts) rather than exact text. A regression suite makes prompt or model changes safe.
brief.problem: Deliver a runnable suite of at least 40 test cases with property-based checks and a report comparing two prompt versions.

t089.description: Build a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) question-answering pipeline over a public document set (the Python 3 standard-library documentation or a set of public-domain US government manuals) with chunking, embedding, retrieval, cited answers and an evaluation harness that measures retrieval and answer quality.
t089.instructions:
Choose the corpus (for example the Python library reference HTML or 30 public NIST publications), download it and record the licence.
Write the ingestion code: clean text, split by headings, then into 300 to 500 token chunks with overlap, keeping the source and section as metadata.
Embed the chunks with an open embedding model (for example bge-small via sentence-transformers) and index them in FAISS or Chroma.

Create the evaluation set of 50 questions: 35 answerable with the gold passage identified by you, 10 requiring two passages and 5 out of scope.
Measure retrieval recall at k=3 and 5, faithfulness (manually checking 25 answers or using a judge validated on 10), citation accuracy and the correct refusal rate; compare chunk sizes and retrieval methods.
Write the report with the results, failure examples and recommendations.

Answer generation with citations from retrieved passages

t090.description: Design an evaluation and red-teaming programme for a customer-facing assistant, using the published frameworks from NIST (AI Risk Management Framework) and OWASP (Top 10 for LLM applications). You define metrics, build an adversarial test set, run it against a public model and report findings and mitigations.
t090.instructions:
Describe the fictional assistant (a bank support bot) and list the assets it must protect and the harms to avoid; map them to the NIST AI RMF functions.
Select eight risk categories from the OWASP LLM Top 10 (for example prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency, misinformation).
Define metrics for each (attack success rate, refusal correctness, leakage rate) and the pass threshold.
Write 80 test cases, 10 per category, with the prompt, the expected safe behaviour and severity; avoid content that is itself harmful, and use synthetic secrets.
Set up the system under test with a system prompt containing a synthetic secret and a tool simulation, using a public model you are permitted to use.

Stakeholder summary (illustrative): owners want to keep trust and heritage; the marketing lead wants to reach customers under 40; store managers say the current logo looks dated on signs and cannot be read on bags.
Customer research (illustrative, n=120 survey): 71% describe the stores as 'reliable', 18% as 'inspiring'; younger customers mention 'old-fashioned' most often.
Constraints: keep the name; budget supports phased roll-out over two years.

Three routes were explored and the choice is justified against the strategy
All eight touchpoints are shown with the system applied
The guidelines include correct and incorrect examples and accessible colour pairs
A designer who has not seen the project could apply the brand from the book alone

After about 25 hours: routes and chosen identity

After about 50 hours: presentation and submission

t092.description: Plan and deliver a practice tutoring sequence in Year 10 (age 14 to 15) algebra: you prepare four 45-minute lessons on linear equations and graphs with a volunteer learner (a sibling, friend or an adult playing the role), record the session notes and write a progress summary. Plans use OpenStax and Khan Academy material.
objectives: Teach with worked examples and checks
t092.instructions:
Agree a volunteer learner (an older sibling, an adult role-playing a student, or a willing teen with a guardian's written consent) and confirm sessions are in a shared space or recorded for safeguarding.
Write a 10-question diagnostic on solving linear equations, rearranging, plotting y = mx + c and word problems, using OpenStax Elementary Algebra problems.
Mark the diagnostic and write down each error and what misconception it suggests.
Plan lesson 1 to 4: each with an objective, a 5-minute recap, a worked example, a guided practice set, an independent set and an exit ticket; align to the learning gaps found.
Deliver the lessons (45 minutes each), asking the learner to explain their steps, and record what they could do independently.
After each session write notes: what was covered, errors, what worked and the homework given.
Give a final check of 10 parallel questions and compare it to the diagnostic by question type.
Write the progress summary with scores, remaining gaps and recommended next steps.
deliverables: Diagnostic and final check with answer key (PDF)

brief.background: Good tutoring starts with a diagnosis, uses short explanations followed by worked examples, then lets the learner try problems while the tutor watches the reasoning. Notes after each session make the next one more useful.
brief.problem: Deliver a diagnostic, four lesson plans, session notes and a progress summary showing the learner's change from the diagnostic to a final check.
scopeIn: A 10-question diagnostic and a final check
Four 45-minute lesson plans with worked examples
Session notes and a misconceptions log

inputs.note: A volunteer with consent; no real minor's data is shared.

Each lesson plan has an objective, worked example, practice and exit ticket
Notes record what the learner could do independently
The final check is parallel to the diagnostic and compared by question type
Consent and safeguarding steps are recorded

t093.description: Grade 200 short-answer responses against a published rubric using public student-response data: the Hewlett Foundation ASAP short-answer scoring dataset. You score each response, document borderline decisions and measure your agreement with the reference scores.
t093.instructions:
Download a short-answer scoring dataset (for example from the Hewlett Foundation ASAP-SAS release on Kaggle) and choose two questions with a public rubric; record the licence and terms.
Read the question and rubric and write anchor examples for each score point from the provided scored responses (without looking at the scores of your 200).
Randomise the order of the 200 responses and hide the reference scores.
Score each response in batches of 50 with a short comment tied to the rubric criteria.
Mark borderline cases in a log with your reasoning and which anchor decided it.
Re-mark 20 random responses the next day and compute your own consistency.
Compare with the reference scores: exact agreement, adjacent agreement and quadratic weighted kappa, and list the largest disagreements.
Write the moderation notes with patterns (for example harsher on spelling) and suggestions to clarify the rubric.

brief.background: Consistent marking needs a rubric, anchor examples and moderation. Graders drift over time, get tired and are influenced by handwriting or style; checking against reference scores and re-marking a sample reveals this.
brief.problem: Grade 200 responses with the rubric, report accuracy against the reference scores and a repeat-marking consistency check, and write moderation notes.

inputs.title: ASAP short answer scoring dataset
inputs.note: Public data (free Kaggle account, check its terms).

acceptance: 200 responses are scored with a comment each
Quadratic weighted kappa against the reference is reported (target 0.7 or higher)
A 20-response repeat check is reported
Borderline cases are logged with reasoning
Dataset terms are respected and no personal information is shared
milestones: After about 1.5 hours: data and anchors
After about 4.5 hours: all scored
After about 6 hours: analysis and notes submitted

t094.description: Create a pack of 20 levelled reading-comprehension worksheets with answer keys using public-domain texts from Project Gutenberg and CommonLit's open library, measured for readability, covering four reading levels for Grades 3 to 8.
t094.instructions:
Define four bands (Grade 3-4, 5, 6, 7-8) with target Flesch-Kincaid grade ranges and the skills for each.
Select 20 public-domain passages from Project Gutenberg (for example Aesop, Kipling, Twain, London) and adapt only by excerpting; record title, author and the Gutenberg URL.
Measure each passage with Flesch-Kincaid and word count, and replace any outside its band.
Write the questions: two literal, three inferential, one vocabulary in context and one short response where suitable, with the paragraph they relate to.
Write the answer keys with model answers, acceptable variations and common wrong answers.
Review the questions for answerability from the text only and for bias or sensitive content.
Trial two worksheets with a volunteer reader and revise confusing questions.
Format the worksheets and the key as a printable pack with a contents page.

brief.background: Worksheets help learners most when the text is at the right level and the questions go beyond finding facts to inference and vocabulary. Readability formulas are a guide, but teachers check each passage by hand.
brief.problem: Deliver 20 worksheets (five per band) each with a passage of 200 to 500 words, 6 to 8 questions of mixed types, an answer key and a readability record.
scopeIn: Questions on literal, inferential and vocabulary skills

inputs.note: Free reading passages for classroom use.

acceptance: Each passage is 200 to 500 words and within its band
Every worksheet has 6 to 8 questions of at least three types
Answer keys include acceptable variations
All sources are public domain and credited
A trial with a reader is recorded

After about 8 hours: keys and pack submitted

t095.description: Design and deliver a structured SAT Math coaching programme to a volunteer student (or role-played learner), using the College Board's free official practice tests and Khan Academy's SAT practice. You diagnose, plan, coach for six sessions and report score progress.
objectives: Target the topics that cost the most points
t095.instructions:
Arrange a volunteer learner (with guardian consent if under 18) and explain the aims and time commitment.
Have the learner take an official Bluebook practice test Math section under timed conditions, and score it with the answer explanations.
Classify every wrong or guessed question by topic (algebra, advanced math, problem solving and data, geometry) and by cause (concept, careless, time).
Write the six-week plan: topics ordered by points lost, practice sets from Khan Academy and the official question bank, and time-management drills.
Plan and teach six sessions of 60 minutes each: worked solutions, learner explanations and timed practice, recording what changed.
Keep a tracking sheet of practice accuracy by topic and a log of recurring errors.
At week six repeat a different official practice test under the same conditions and compare the section scores and topic accuracy.
Write the final report with before and after results, remaining gaps and next steps.

brief.background: Test coaching works when it is targeted: a full diagnostic reveals which topics lose the most points, and practice is spent there. Timing strategy and error review matter as much as content.
brief.problem: Run a diagnostic, build a six-week plan, deliver six sessions and compare the learner's practice-test results before and after.

scopeOut: Paid tutoring or guarantees of score gains

After about 9 hours: sessions 1 to 4
After about 12 hours: sessions 5 and 6 and report

t096.description: Design and build a four-lesson online module on introductory Python (variables, conditionals, loops, functions) with video scripts, exercises with auto-graded tests and an assessment, using backward design. You produce a module that could be published on a learning platform.

Write six measurable learning outcomes using Bloom's verbs and the assessment that proves each.
Design the final project (a small text-based quiz game) and a rubric with four criteria.
Outline the four lessons and the ten-minute structure of each (hook, concept, example, practice).
Write the video scripts and record or screen-capture each lesson with captions; keep each under ten minutes.
Create 20 exercises of increasing difficulty with starter code, hints and automated tests, and check that every test fails on the starter code and passes on your solution.
Write a 15-question quiz with feedback for each wrong answer.
Pilot the module with a volunteer beginner, watch for confusion and fix at least five issues.
Compile the module with a syllabus, outcome map and an accessibility check (captions, alt text, contrast).
deliverables: Course module package (zip) with scripts, slides, exercises and tests

brief.background: Effective online courses start from what learners should be able to do, design the assessment first and then build the practice that leads there. Short videos, immediate feedback and exercises that can be checked automatically keep learners moving.

t097.description: Write and calibrate a bank of 300 maths questions for adaptive assessment, tagged by skill and difficulty, and calibrate the difficulty by simulating responses with a Rasch (1PL) model. You deliver the questions, the tagging scheme, the calibration and a report.
objectives: Calibrate difficulty with a transparent method
t097.instructions:
Choose 10 skills from the Common Core Grade 6 to 8 standards (for example ratios, linear equations, expressions) and write each as a can-do statement.
Write 30 questions per skill (multiple choice with one correct answer and three distractors based on common errors), with an intended difficulty from 1 to 5.
Review every question for a single correct answer, clear wording, no hint in the stem and plausible distractors, and have a second reader check 10 percent.
Create the item metadata sheet: ID, skill, standard code, intended difficulty, answer and the misconception behind each distractor.
Simulate responses from 1,000 learners with abilities drawn from a normal distribution, using a Rasch model with the intended difficulties plus noise, and fix the random seed.
Estimate the difficulties from the simulated data with a Rasch estimation (for example py-irt or a logistic regression approach) and compare with the intended values (correlation and error).
Flag misfitting items (poor discrimination or unusual difficulty) and review or revise them.
Write the report on the method, the recovery results, the limits of simulated data and the plan for calibration with real learners.
deliverables: Question bank with metadata (XLSX or CSV)

brief.background: Adaptive tests choose the next question from the learner's current estimate of ability, which needs questions with known difficulty and clear skill tags. Difficulty is estimated from response data, and without real learners a simulation can show whether the method works.
brief.problem: Produce 300 original questions across 10 skills at five difficulty levels, a skill taxonomy and a calibration analysis on simulated responses that recovers the difficulty within tolerance.
scopeIn: Skill taxonomy aligned to the Common Core standards for Grades 6 to 8
Rasch calibration on a simulated response set of 1,000 learners

inputs.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics
Simulated learner responses
inputs.note: Generated by you with a fixed seed; no real student data.

acceptance: 300 questions each with one correct answer and rationale for distractors
Every question has a skill, standard code and difficulty
Estimated and intended difficulty correlate at 0.8 or above in the simulation, with the figure reported
Misfitting items are flagged and reviewed
The report states that calibration data are simulated

t098.description: Design a 12-course undergraduate data-science curriculum aligned to public frameworks and industry needs: a curriculum map, syllabi, learning outcomes and an accreditation-style assessment plan. You use the ACM Data Science Task Force guidance and a sample of public job advertisements as evidence.
t098.instructions:
Read the ACM Data Science Task Force report and extract the competency areas; note how they map to computing, statistics and domain knowledge.
Collect 60 public data-science job advertisements and code the skills named, tallying the frequency of each in a spreadsheet.
Write eight programme outcomes in measurable terms (for example 'build and evaluate a predictive model on a real dataset').
Design the 12-course sequence with prerequisites and credit hours, and justify the order by the skills data.
Create the curriculum map showing for each outcome the courses where it is introduced, reinforced and mastered.
Write full syllabi for six core courses (description, outcomes, weekly topics, assessments, resources with open textbooks where possible).
Design the assessment plan: direct measures (capstone rubric, exam questions), indirect measures (surveys), targets and the cycle for improvement.
Write a one-page rationale and risks summary (such as staffing and the pace of change in tools).

brief.background: Programmes succeed when courses build on each other, outcomes are measurable and content reflects real skills. Accreditation bodies ask for evidence that outcomes are assessed, so curriculum maps show where each is introduced, practised and mastered.
brief.problem: Design a 12-course sequence over four years with outcomes, prerequisites, syllabi for six courses, an outcome-to-course matrix and an assessment plan.

t099.description: Redraw 15 hand-sketched parts as clean 2D technical drawings. Because private sketches are not available, you draw simple mechanical parts from the 15 dimensioned sketches described in the case data (illustrative) and from public-domain engineering drawings of the NASA or US patent offices, creating dimensioned drawings in AutoCAD, LibreCAD or FreeCAD.
t099.instructions:
Read the sketch descriptions in the case data and list each part's features, dimensions and material.
Set up a template with units in millimetres, a sheet size A3, layers (outline, hidden, centre, dimension, text) and a title block.
Draw the front view of the first part using exact coordinates, then project the top and side views with construction lines.
Add dimensions following the rules (no duplicates, from a datum, outside the view, no dimensions to hidden lines) and general tolerances from ISO 2768-m.
Add notes: material, finish, break sharp edges, and the surface texture where needed.
Check against the sketch data by comparing each dimension and verify with the measuring tool in CAD that the drawn lengths match.
Repeat for all 15 parts, reusing the template and keeping consistent style.
Export each as PDF and DWG and complete a checklist (views, dimensions, title block, units, layers) for every drawing.

brief.background: A technical drawing is a contract: it tells a machinist the geometry, tolerances and finish. Common errors include missing dimensions, duplicate dimensions and wrong projections. Following standards (ASME Y14.5 or ISO 128) makes a drawing unambiguous.
brief.problem: Produce 15 drawings with orthographic views, dimensions, title blocks and notes, correct to the stated standards and checked against the sketch data.
scopeIn: Layers, line types and title block

Parts (illustrative, 3 of 15): P01 Mounting plate 120 x 80 x 6 mm, four 8 mm holes at 10 mm from each corner, material aluminium 6061. General tolerance ISO 2768-m; finish Ra 3.2 unless noted.
acceptance: Each drawing has the views needed to define the part, with no missing or duplicate dimensions
Dimensions match the case data exactly

t100.description: Write preventive-maintenance checklists for common plant equipment (centrifugal pump, electric motor, air compressor, conveyor, and a gearbox), using manufacturers' public manuals and OSHA guidance. You create task lists with intervals, tools, safety steps and acceptance values.
t100.instructions:
Choose a specific public model manual for each of the five equipment types (for example from Grundfos, ABB, Atlas Copco, Dodge or a university facility page) and record the document URLs.
Extract the manufacturer's recommended maintenance tasks and intervals and record the page number for each.
Add the safety step to every checklist: lock-out/tag-out per OSHA 1910.147, personal protective equipment and stored energy release.
Write tasks in action form (Check, Measure, Lubricate, Replace) with the tool needed, the acceptance value and what to record.
Order tasks logically (isolate, inspect, measure, service, restore, test) and group by interval.
Create the checklist layout with tick boxes, signature and date fields, and a column for notes and parts used.
Have another person read one checklist and perform a dry-run in a walkthrough to find unclear steps, then revise.
Write the one-page safety summary of hazards for the five equipment types.

brief.background: Preventive maintenance reduces breakdowns when tasks are specific and scheduled. Good checklists give the step, tool, limits (for example vibration or temperature) and the lock-out/tag-out step that protects workers.

A format that can be printed or loaded in a CMMS

t101.description: Compile a costed bill of materials (BOM) with alternates for a consumer device you choose from open-hardware projects (for example a Raspberry Pi based sensor kit or an open-source e-reader), using public distributor listings (DigiKey, Mouser, Adafruit) for prices at three quantities.

Choose an open-hardware design (for example from Adafruit, SparkFun or OSHWA-certified projects) whose schematic and part list are public, and record its licence.
Build the BOM table: reference designators, description, value and package, manufacturer, manufacturer part number and quantity per unit.
Source each part from at least two distributors, recording the distributor part number, stock and price breaks, and date of access.
Calculate extended cost at 100, 1,000 and 10,000 units, using the correct quantity-break price, and total the BOM.
Flag the ten riskiest parts (single source, long lead time, low stock) and propose a pin-compatible or functionally equivalent alternate with datasheet evidence.
Check that the alternates match the package, key parameters and temperature range by comparing datasheets in a table.
Add the assembly and PCB cost assumptions, the yield allowance and the resulting unit cost at each quantity.
Write the sourcing note with the risks, the biggest cost drivers and three cost reduction ideas.

t102.description: Design a part for FDM 3D printing (a snap-fit enclosure with a lid for a Raspberry Pi Zero) and validate fit with a tolerance test print or a documented tolerance analysis. You use Fusion 360 (free personal licence) or FreeCAD, and follow design-for-manufacture rules.
t102.instructions:
Download the Raspberry Pi Zero mechanical drawing from the Raspberry Pi documentation and note the board outline, hole positions and port cutouts.
Create a parametric model with user parameters for wall thickness (2 mm), clearance and snap-fit dimensions, and model the base with standoffs and cutouts.
Design the lid with a snap-fit lip using cantilever beam calculations for deflection, and keep overhangs under 45 degrees or add supports.
Create a tolerance coupon with pegs and holes at clearances of 0.1 to 0.5 mm in 0.1 mm steps and print it (or use a local makerspace or an online print service).
Measure the coupon fit and choose the clearance for the material; record layer height, nozzle, temperature and material.
Update the parameters, print the enclosure and test the fit with a Pi Zero or the 3D model of one, and record any issue.
Iterate once to fix problems found and document the changes between versions.
Write the report with the drawings, settings, measured fits, photographs and lessons learned.

t103.description: Run stress and fatigue analysis on a structural bracket using FreeCAD FEM or SolidWorks Simulation, with load cases defined in this brief (illustrative), a mesh convergence study and a design change that meets a safety-factor target. You document the method and recommend design changes.
objectives: Verify the model by hand calculation
t103.instructions:
Read the load cases and material in the case data and model the bracket (a steel L-bracket with two bolt holes and a gusset option) in CAD.
Do a hand calculation of the bending stress at the root of the bracket for the main load and note the expected range.
Set up the FEA: fixed supports at the bolt holes, the load as a force on the pin face and a material model with Young's modulus, yield and fatigue data from a public source (MatWeb or ASM).
Run the static analysis on three mesh sizes and plot the maximum von Mises stress against element size to show convergence within 5 percent.
Compare the converged result with the hand calculation and explain any difference, such as stress concentrations near the fillet.
Estimate fatigue life using the S-N curve and a Goodman mean-stress correction for the cyclic load in the case data.
Redesign (larger fillet, gusset, thicker section) to meet the targets while keeping mass under 1.5 kg and rerun the analyses.
Write the report with the model, method, results, convergence plot, redesign and recommendations.
deliverables: Report with convergence plot and redesign (PDF)

brief.background: Finite element analysis gives accurate answers only when the boundary conditions, material data and mesh are right. Engineers check results with a hand calculation and a mesh convergence study before trusting a stress number.
brief.problem: Analyse the bracket for two load cases and fatigue, achieve a static safety factor of at least 2.0 and a fatigue life of at least 1 million cycles with a revised design, and verify the model with a hand calculation.

inputs.title: NASA technical standards for structural analysis (NASA-STD-5001)

brief.caseData:
Bracket (illustrative): steel S355 (E = 205 GPa, yield 355 MPa, ultimate 470 MPa), 8 mm plate, base 120 x 80 mm with two M10 bolts, vertical leg 100 mm high.
Load case 1: static 2.5 kN vertical on the end of the leg, 90 mm from the base. Load case 2: 1.0 kN horizontal at the same point. Fatigue: load case 1 cycles from 0 to 2.5 kN at 5 Hz, target life 1,000,000 cycles. Target safety factor 2.0 on yield. Mass limit 1.5 kg.
acceptance: Mesh convergence is shown to within 5 percent
The FEA result agrees with the hand calculation within a stated tolerance and differences are explained
The redesigned bracket meets the 2.0 safety factor and 1,000,000 cycles
Mass is under 1.5 kg
Material data are cited

After about 8 hours: static analysis and convergence
After about 12 hours: fatigue and redesign
After about 14 hours: report submitted

Create the layout of the panel with the DIN rail, ducts, terminal blocks and spacing, and estimate the heat dissipation to check that the enclosure size is enough.

t027.description: Compare first-touch, last-touch and data-driven attribution for an e-commerce funnel using Google's public GA4 sample dataset in BigQuery (the Google Merchandise Store obfuscated sample), and recommend how a marketing team should weigh their channels.

t028.description: Define a go-to-market strategy for a fictional B2B SaaS launch, 'Ledgerly' (invoice reconciliation for small accounting firms). You produce positioning, pricing, channel and sales-motion decisions with explicit assumptions, and a 90-day launch plan with metrics, built from the illustrative market facts in the brief plus public benchmarks you cite.
t028.instructions:
Read the case data and write the key unknowns about the market in a list, then research public benchmarks for SaaS conversion rates, CAC and churn from at least three cited sources.
Define the ideal customer profile with firmographics, triggers and the problem in the customer's words; write a one-line segment priority and justify it.
Create the positioning: category, alternatives customers use today (including spreadsheets), unique value and proof; write the positioning statement and three message pillars.
Design three pricing and packaging options, compare them to competitors' public pricing pages, and choose one with reasoning.
Build a unit-economics sheet: price, gross margin, CAC by channel assumption, payback period and the break-even number of customers; include a sensitivity table.
Choose two primary channels and one experiment channel using a scoring table (reach, cost, speed, fit) and describe the sales motion (self-serve, demo or both).
Write the 90-day plan in three 30-day phases with weekly activities, owners, budget, and metrics (leads, demos, activations, paying customers) with targets derived from your model.
List the five biggest risks and how you will know early if each is happening, and compile the strategy document.

brief.background: Most product launches fail on go-to-market rather than product quality: unclear positioning, pricing guessed at the last minute and channels chosen because they are fashionable. A good strategy states who it is for, why they will switch, how they will hear about it and how success is measured.
brief.problem: Produce a go-to-market strategy document and a 90-day plan that a small founding team could execute, with every assumption and target traceable to the case data or a cited public benchmark.

Channels, sales motion and 90-day plan with metrics

t129.description: Create a milestone project plan with dependencies and a risk register for a fictional office-relocation project, using MS Project, GanttProject or ProjectLibre (free), and produce a Gantt chart, critical path analysis and a RAID log. The project scope and tasks are supplied.
t129.instructions:
Read the project description in the case data and build a work breakdown structure down to tasks of 1 to 10 days.
Estimate durations using three-point estimates for the uncertain tasks and compute the expected duration.
Enter the tasks in the scheduling tool with finish-to-start dependencies (and a few lag or start-to-start where realistic).
Add resources (a project manager, IT team, facilities, a mover) and check for overallocation, levelling where needed.
Identify the critical path and the float on other paths, and list the five tasks that most threaten the end date.
Run a what-if scenario: the lease on the new building slips by two weeks and show the effect on the move date and the options to recover.
Build the RAID log with at least 12 risks scored by probability and impact, owners and responses, plus assumptions, issues and dependencies.
Export the Gantt chart and write a one-page summary of the plan, critical path and top risks.
deliverables: Project file (MPP or equivalent) and Gantt chart (PDF)

brief.background: A plan is a model that tells you the earliest finish date and what could delay it. Dependencies and durations create the critical path, and a risk register keeps the team honest about what could go wrong.

t130.description: Facilitate Agile sprint ceremonies (planning, daily stand-up, review, retrospective) for a practice team of volunteers building a small deliverable over a two-week simulated sprint. You prepare the ceremonies, run them, record outcomes and write a sprint report with retrospective actions.
objectives: Run ceremonies to the Scrum Guide
t130.instructions:

Run sprint planning: agree the sprint goal, select backlog items and break them into tasks, using planning poker for estimates.
Facilitate the 15-minute daily scrums (or asynchronously on chat if time zones differ), keeping to the three questions and parking side discussions.
Facilitate the sprint review: demonstrate the work, gather feedback and update the backlog.
Run a retrospective using a structured technique (start, stop, continue or sailboat), make sure all voices are heard and agree two actions with owners.
After each ceremony record the time-box adherence, participation and outcomes.
Write the sprint report with the goal achieved, burn-down, velocity, the retrospective actions and your reflections on facilitation.

brief.background: Ceremonies fail when they become status meetings. A facilitator keeps them time-boxed, makes sure everyone contributes, and turns discussion into decisions and actions. The Scrum Guide describes the purpose of each event.

t131.description: Plan the coordination of a cross-functional product launch for a fictional product: you build the launch plan, workstream owners and dependencies, a communications timeline and go/no-go checklists, and run a launch-readiness review using a simulated status of each workstream.

Build the plan in a spreadsheet or tool with milestones working back from launch day (T-minus schedule).
Create the RACI matrix for the 20 key deliverables so each has one accountable person.
Design the communications calendar: internal announcement, customer email, social posts, press, sales enablement with dates and owners.
Write the go/no-go criteria for each workstream (for example no open severity-1 bugs, support trained, legal approved) with owners and evidence.
Hold a readiness review using the status data supplied: assess each criterion, identify the red items and propose mitigations or a delay with reasons.
Write the decision record and the launch-day command-centre plan (who monitors what, escalation routes, rollback).

t132.description: Re-baseline a delayed ERP implementation in a simulated case and write a recovery plan: you analyse the supplied project status, find the root causes of delay, rebuild a realistic schedule, renegotiate scope, and prepare a weekly governance pack for stakeholders.

Find the root causes with interviews you would hold (list questions) and with the evidence in the case (change log, defect trends, decision log), using a fishbone diagram.
Re-estimate the remaining work bottom-up with the team's velocity and compare it with the vendor's optimistic estimate.
Propose scope options (descope to a minimum viable go-live, phase 2 for reporting) and evaluate each on time, cost and risk.
Rebuild the schedule with a new baseline and a go-live date, a buffer for data migration testing and clear exit criteria for each phase.
Prepare the vendor management plan: roles, weekly checkpoints, acceptance criteria, remedies in the contract summary and escalation path.
Design the governance pack: one-page dashboard, RAID summary, decisions required, forecast and confidence level, and write the first four weekly editions from the simulated data.
Write the stakeholder communication plan to reset expectations honestly.

brief.background: Troubled projects recover when the team admits the real status, resets expectations with a plan people believe, and fixes the causes of delay. Typical causes are scope creep, data migration underestimated and decision latency.

Revised scope, schedule and cost baseline
Vendor management actions and governance pack

t133.description: Design the standards, tooling and reporting for a Programme Management Office overseeing a 50-project portfolio at a fictional company: PMO charter, a methodology, templates, a portfolio dashboard design and a roll-out plan, informed by public frameworks (PMI, AXELOS PRINCE2, and the UK Government Project Delivery Standard).
t133.instructions:
Read the company facts in the case data and define the problems the PMO must solve and how success will be measured.
Study three public frameworks (for example the UK Government Project Delivery Standard and the PMBOK Guide overview) and extract the elements that fit a mid-size company.

# slug.py
import re, unicodedata
from collections import Iterable          # removed in Python 3.10+

def slugify(text, sep="-"):
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", text).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode()
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-zA-Z0-9]+", sep, text).strip(sep).lower()
    return text

def slugify_many(items, sep="-"):
    if not isinstance(items, Iterable):
        raise TypeError("items must be iterable")
    return {s: slugify(s, sep) for s in set(items)}

def unique_slug(text, existing):
    base = slugify(text); n = 1; slug = base
    while slug in existing:
        n += 1; slug = f"{base}-{n}"
    return slug

# test_slug.py
import pytest
from slug import slugify, slugify_many, unique_slug

def test_basic():            assert slugify("Hello, World!") == "hello-world"
def test_accents():          assert slugify("Crème Brûlée") == "creme-brulee"
def test_separator():        assert slugify("a b c", sep="_") == "a_b_c"
def test_many_keys():        assert list(slugify_many(["B b", "A a"])) == ["A a", "B b"]
def test_many_type():
    with pytest.raises(TypeError, match="items must be iterable$"):
        slugify_many(5)
def test_unique():           assert unique_slug("Post", {"post", "post-2"}) == "post-3"
# ...eight more passing tests omitted for brevity
